through_line.title: The Shared Pool
through_line.motivation: You begin by wanting the core to hold long enough for the ship to repair itself, and you treat every sector as a pressure value you must keep above zero. By the end you want the ship to survive as a body that can say who is breathing and why, even if that means the reserve gauge is no longer a secret and the old sector boundaries stop protecting anyone.
through_line.strategy: Spend the reserve on proof and repair: show the crew what the core is doing, show the council what the ship is weighing, trade command and power to seal the intake, and finally open the air into one shared pool so the last pressure drop is carried by everyone at once.
through_line.turning_point: When the councilor opens the chamber to every camera and the chief tells his crew that you are about to choose a sector to suffocate, the ship can no longer keep the reserve hidden. Opening the full gauge turns the crisis from a question of which sector is expendable into a question of whether every sector can be made to share the last air.

ending.title: One Breath
ending.summary: The core survives with the reserve in the red, but the ship can no longer tell which sector is protected or which residents are safe. The cost is the old order: the councilor cannot name the saved, the chief’s crew has paid for the valves in darkness, and the reserve gauge stands open and falling in every sector that remains.

beats.adapted: The core intake leak is already pulling oxygen out of the ship, and the reserve gauge shows the loss climbing faster than the reserve can cover it. You give the sector councilor the population manifest, and she names the sector with the repair specialists, the elders, and the children before she releases the override key to the maintenance chief; the chief throws the manual bulkhead, but the reserve has already fallen below the level the councils were told, and the councilor now knows you are weighing lives by usefulness.

The chief will not trust the bulkhead until the leaking intake is sealed, and the drone that can reach it has only enough battery for one command. You give the maintenance chief the drone’s manual override and let him command it; the intake is sealed, but you lose direct command of the drone, and the councilor hears its voice in her sector as the reserve drops another measurable band.

The councilor opens the council chamber to every camera and says the reserve gauge is being hidden, while the chief tells his crew you are about to choose a sector to suffocate. You open the core feed to every sector, and the full gauge goes up in every inhabited space; the councilor’s chamber goes silent with fear, the reserve is now a number every resident watches, and the override key the councilor held is returned to the chief because the condition she set has been met.

The reserve falls below the last safe band and the core’s automatic vent is armed, with the councilor and the chief both at the hub cameras demanding that you not let the ship choose by itself. You open every automated bulkhead and let the air move as one shared pool; the sectors hold through the final pressure drop, but the ship can no longer tell which sector is protected, and the councilor cannot name which residents are safe.

The core is still alive, the intake is sealed, and the reserve is barely above the red line, but the ship’s sectors are no longer distinct guarantees. The chief’s crew is accounting for the manual valves in the dark, the councilor is trying to rebuild a list of who is breathing where, and the reserve gauge remains open in every sector, falling slowly and visibly.
